claims.claim: A stock is a type of security that gives the stockholder a share of ownership in a company; stocks are also called equities — the working definition used in the lesson, attributed to SEC Investor.gov.

Stock owners earn in two main ways: capital appreciation, which occurs when a stock rises in price, and dividend payments, which come when the company distributes some of its earnings to stockholders.
A dividend is a portion of a company's profit paid to shareholders; public companies that pay dividends usually do so on a fixed schedule.
Stock prices move down as well as up; there is no guarantee that the company whose stock you hold will grow and do well, so you can lose money you invest in stocks.
Even when companies are not in danger of failing, their stock prices may fluctuate up or down; large-company stocks as a group have lost money on average about one out of every three years.

Stocks are usually one part of an investor's holdings, not the whole portfolio; the risks of stock holdings can be offset in part by investing in a number of different stocks and in other kinds of assets.

Investors can buy and sell stocks through a broker (a brokerage account) or through a stock fund that invests primarily in stocks; in general, investment money is often held in a brokerage or advisory account.

Stock investing is for long horizons: investors willing to stick with stocks over long periods of time, say fifteen years, have generally been rewarded with strong, positive returns, and money for long-term goals such as retirement will not be used for decades.
Investing has no set rate of return, all investments involve some degree of risk, and investors should allow for market fluctuations over time — the basis of the lesson's honest framing.
Return from an asset may come from an increase in the asset's value or from the asset's interest or dividend payments to those who own it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a well-known company's stock is effectively safe
positions: Investor.gov: even when companies are not in danger of failing, their stock prices may fluctuate up or down, and large-company stocks as a group have lost money on average about one out of every three years.
Informal marketing and casual advice sometimes imply that famous, established companies are safe places for money.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states plainly that prices fall as well as rise for any stock and that no company's future is guaranteed; the honest note is kept, with no 'safe stock' claim.

positions: Investor.gov: investors willing to stick with stocks over long periods (about 15 years) have generally been rewarded with strong, positive returns.
The same regulator notes prices move down as well as up and that you can lose money if you sell when the price is below what you paid.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents long horizons as the general practice for stock investing and notes that money needed soon cannot afford to wait out a fall; it gives no advice about specific accounts or products.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether dividend payments are guaranteed to continue
positions: Investor.gov: dividends are a portion of a company's profit paid to shareholders, and public companies that pay them usually do so on a fixed schedule.
Casual descriptions of 'dividend stocks' sometimes imply steady, dependable income regardless of company performance.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says some companies share profits with owners and frames dividends as one way to earn, not a promise; no dividend is presented as guaranteed.
